how-much-to-charge-to-replace-a-sewer-li.text:
← Sewer line replacement bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a sewer line

A published $125-a-foot special treats 40 feet under a lawn as the same job as 80 feet under a driveway with two laterals and a 6-foot bury. It is not. Hydro-jet calculators price cleaning an existing line. Septic calculators price a tank lid and extra gallons. Replacing the pipe is a method, a surface, and the laterals you have to reconnect. Quoting all of that from a per-foot special is how the first sawcut eats the field margin.

A job with the same footage can cost much more

Each extra foot of hard surface is time that never appears on the brochure. On the sample rates a 40-foot open-cut under lawn with one cleanout prices about $3,407 ($85 per foot, 13.3 crew-hours, walk-away $2,385). The same shop’s 80-foot open-cut under a driveway with two laterals prices about $10,368 ($130 per foot, 40.8 hours). Half of that driveway bid is restoration — labor, asphalt patch, and the dump ticket. Matching the yard job’s $85-a-foot special on the driveway run is how that job becomes a loss.

Trenchless wins when you would have to put the driveway back

Pipe bursting restores pits, not the whole slab. On the same 80-foot driveway run the sample rates price bursting at about $5,697 — $4,671 less than open-cut. CIPP lining the same run prices about $8,593. Open-cut is still competitive on short lawn work: lining that 40-foot yard job prices about $4,659 because the wet-out liner is not free. Treating every run as one per-foot number is how the method that looked cheapest on paper is not the one that keeps the margin.

A liner with laterals is not automatically the cheap no-dig job

A 120-foot 6-inch CIPP liner with three laterals and an occupied-house bypass is not the 80-foot driveway burst plus 50%. On the sample rates that liner prices about $17,302 ($144 per foot, 15.1 crew-hours). Restoration is zero; the laterals and the liner footage are the bid. A 60-foot pipe-burst under sidewalk with two pits prices about $5,518 ($92 per foot). Neither number lives in a $125-a-foot special.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $42/h tech loaded at 35% payroll burden is $56.70. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is arithmetic on the rates you type. It is not a plumbing specification, a code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommendation of open-cut versus trenchless. Depth, soil, laterals, and what the jurisdiction will accept still decide the method. Verify every figure against your own takeoff.

No warranty. This free page is not plumbing, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. It is hosted best-effort with no SLA: it may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Open the bid calculator to price a specific run.

Common questions

How much to charge to replace a sewer line?

Charge from the method (open-cut, pipe bursting, or CIPP lining), the run footage, bury depth, laterals, cleanouts, the surface you have to put back, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 40-foot open-cut under lawn at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $3,407 — about $85 per foot.

When is trenchless cheaper than open-cut?

When the run sits under a driveway, sidewalk, or street. On the sample rates an 80-foot open-cut under a driveway with two laterals prices around $10,368, half of that in restoration. Pipe bursting the same run prices around $5,697. The per-foot special never sees the sawcut.

How much to charge for CIPP lining?

A liner is not a burst and a burst is not an open-cut. On the sample rates a 120-foot 6-inch CIPP job with three laterals and an occupied-house bypass prices around $17,302 ($144 per foot, 15.1 crew-hours). Laterals are the expensive part of lining; restoration is usually zero.

        Common questions

        Is $129.60 a foot a rate I can quote from?

        No — it is the finished price divided by the run, not a unit rate. The default job prices at $10,368.03 over 80 feet, but a large share of that is the excavator mobilization, the permit, the connection at each end, and restoration, none of which double when the run does. A 160-foot replacement is not $20,736. Use the per-foot figure to compare against a competitor’s per-foot quote on a similar run, then price the actual job from its own depth and access.

        Where do 40.75 hours go on a single sewer line?

        Almost none of it is pipe-laying. The hours cover excavation to depth, shoring and spoil handling, the tie-in at the house and at the main, backfill in lifts, compaction, and the inspection wait — at a $56.70 loaded rate that is $2,310.53 of labor against $3,655 of material. Depth is the variable that moves this most: the same 80 feet at eight feet deep is a very different day from four feet.

        Why is the permit only $150 on a $10,000 job?

        Because it is the permit fee itself, not the cost of complying with it. The inspection wait, the required bedding material, and the tie-in method your jurisdiction specifies are all in the hours and materials above. Treat the $150 as a placeholder to replace with your own authority’s schedule — some charge per connection, some by run length, and a few require a separate right-of-way permit for the portion in the street.

        Does this include putting the yard back?

        Only the backfill and compaction. Replacing driveway, sidewalk, mature landscaping, or irrigation that sat over the trench is not in the default number, and on a front-yard run it is frequently the largest surprise on the final invoice. Price restoration separately and say so on the proposal, so the homeowner is not comparing your complete number against someone else’s excavation-only one.

vs-a-flat-per-foot-price.html.text:
← Sewer Line Replacement Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat "$125-a-foot" price

"$125 a foot" is not a price for a sewer replacement — it is a price for one specific depth, one surface, and zero laterals, quietly applied to every run the truck pulls up to.

What a flat per-foot price is

A per-foot number is the fastest way to quote: one figure on a website or a phone call, multiplied by the tape measurement and read back as the price. Homeowners shop it because it turns a sewer replacement into something they can compare the way they compare a fence or a driveway — by length alone.

The number behind it was set for one job — one method (usually open-cut), one depth, one surface (usually lawn), zero laterals, zero access pits — and then reused for every run afterward, whether or not the next job looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the replacement method (open-cut excavation, pipe bursting, or CIPP lining), the run footage and how much of that run sits under hard surface, bury depth, pipe diameter, the number of laterals, cleanouts, and access pits, whether the house stays occupied, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the excavation or trenchless labor and the restoration hours separately, and returns a price per foot, a restoration share, and a walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this run, not a generic one.

What a flat per-foot price doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate per foot whether the run is 40 feet under a lawn at a 5-foot bury or 80 feet under a driveway at a 6-foot bury with two laterals — a several-times difference in restoration and tie-in cost for the same word "sewer replacement". Prices excavation, laterals, and restoration from the entered footage, depth, surface, and lateral count, so the two runs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "a sewer line" as one length of pipe, with no separate line for the asphalt, concrete, or spoils-dump cost a driveway or street run drags in on top of the excavation itself. Times hard-surface restoration and spoils disposal as their own line items, only when that surface is entered, so that cost shows up instead of being absorbed into a blended per-foot rate.
Uses one method's labor curve (usually open-cut) for every job, so it cannot say whether pipe bursting or CIPP would actually keep more margin on a given run once pits, liner, and restoration are counted. Prices open-cut, pipe bursting, and CIPP as their own labor and material shapes, so the same run can be compared across methods instead of assumed into one.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "per-foot rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the crew a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when an owner asks to match a cheaper per-foot figure from a competitor's postcard. Reports the walk-away price and the restoration share of the job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat per-foot price is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one run it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about what a given line can carry; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-foot price get a sewer replacement wrong?

Because labor and restoration cost scale with depth, surface, and laterals, not with footage alone. A 40-foot run under a lawn at a 5-foot bury is a different job from an 80-foot run under a driveway with two laterals and a 6-foot bury — the second carries hard-surface restoration and lateral tie-ins the first has none of. A flat per-foot number quotes both the same length the same price and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a per-foot special usually leave out entirely?

Surface restoration and depth. A per-foot rate built on a shallow lawn run has nowhere to put the extra excavation hours a deeper bury adds, or the asphalt, concrete, or spoils-dump cost a driveway or sidewalk run drags in on top of the pipe itself. A crew pricing off the special alone is short before the trench is open.

Does trenchless change what a per-foot price should be?

Often, and not in a fixed direction. Pipe bursting and CIPP lining trade excavation labor for setup time, liner or burst-head cost, and access pits, and they can avoid tearing up a driveway or a street entirely. Whether that nets out cheaper than open-cut on a given run depends on the run's own depth, surface, and lateral count — exactly the inputs a single per-foot number was never built to hold.

Is a flat per-foot price ever the right way to quote a sewer replacement?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same method, same depth, same surface, no laterals beyond what the rate assumed — a flat number can land close. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know which band a given run is in and neither does the crew until the job is scoped.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, disposal fees, or what competitors charge. It takes the method, footage, surface, depth, laterals, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a price per foot, a restoration share, and a walk-away price for the run you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-foot price is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

Open the Sewer Line Replacement Bid Calculator and price your own run, or read the pricing walkthrough.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is account-based field-service software for running a trade business across dispatch, technicians, and invoicing. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this sewer run cost, given its method, footage, depth, laterals, and the surface that has to go back, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is field-service management software founded in 2012 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan and headquartered in Glendale, California, built for residential and commercial trade contractors across plumbing, HVAC, electrical, and related trades. It combines customer records, dispatch and scheduling, technician mobile tools, estimating and sales presentation, invoicing, payments, inventory, and reporting into one system meant to run a whole contracting business across every truck and every job, and it listed on Nasdaq in December 2024. It is sold as an ongoing account for the company rather than as a single-job tool. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented, non-numeric identity — a field-service management platform for trade contractors, sold as an ongoing account — is stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not hold customer records, dispatch trucks, run a technician app, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the replacement method (open-cut excavation, pipe bursting, or CIPP lining), the run footage and how much of it sits under hard surface, bury depth, pipe diameter, the number of laterals, cleanouts, and access pits, whether the house stays occupied and needs a bypass, plus loaded wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the crew hours the job actually consumes, the price per foot, the share of the bid that is surface restoration rather than pipe, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or ServiceTitan?

They do different jobs, and a plumbing or sewer-repair shop of any size will likely end up touching both eventually. Does this calculator decide whether a line can be burst or lined?

No. It prices the method you pick; it does not pick the method. The calculator's value is showing what each method costs on the same run once that call has been made, including the surface restoration that often decides which one keeps the margin.
